title: Sharpless 2-188 (Sh2-188)
caption: The planetary nebula Sharpless 2-188, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector/University of Alaska Anchorage, H. Schweiker/WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: A nearly circular nebula glows much more brightly along its lower-left side, while faint wisps trail away in the opposite direction. This is Sharpless 2-188, or Sh2-188, an unusual planetary nebula in the constellation Cassiopeia.

Planetary nebulae are shells of gas thrown off by stars late in their lives. Here, the expanding gas is crashing into the ambient gas of the interstellar medium, the thin material that fills the space between stars.

The lopsided brightness has a simple cause. The central star is moving rapidly towards the southeast, the lower left in this view, and that side of the nebula shines much more brightly as it pushes into the surrounding gas. Faint wisps of gas can also be traced on the opposite side.

understand.summary: Deep exposures with the Mosaic 1.1 camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in cyan.
filters: 499 nm · Optical Olll (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
656 nm · Optical Ha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: Narrow filters and deep exposures reveal faint gas that the eye could not see.

explore: The picture was made to show off what the newly installed CCD detectors could do in the Mosaic 1.1 camera, which is mounted on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. In this view, north points up.
alt: A nearly circular nebula, much brighter at lower left, with faint wisps extending towards the upper right.
